answer:
**Extrinsics answer where the camera is; intrinsics answer how its rays become pixels.** Extrinsic rotation and translation transform a world point into camera coordinates. Intrinsics then scale the projected coordinates by focal lengths and shift them by the principal point. Lens distortion adjusts the ideal pinhole result to match real optics. [1](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d9/d0c/group__calib3d.html)

For a camera-frame point (X,Y,Z), the undistorted horizontal coordinate is approximately $u=f_xX/Z+c_x$ when skew is zero. If X=1 m, Z=5 m, $f_x=1000$ pixels, and $c_x=640$, then u=840 pixels. Moving the point twice as far away with the same X halves its offset from the principal point.

Radial distortion changes displacement with distance from the optical center; tangential distortion captures effects such as lens decentering. Calibration estimates these parameters using known geometry observed from several viewpoints. Held-out views help reveal whether the fitted model generalizes beyond the calibration images.

**Coordinate conventions are part of the answer.** State whether the transform maps world to camera or the reverse, and use consistent units. Cropping shifts the principal point; resizing changes focal lengths expressed in pixels. Focus or zoom changes may invalidate a previous calibration. Inspect residuals across the image, especially corners, rather than trusting only one average reprojection error.

**Technical details and references.**

Intrinsics map camera-frame rays to image coordinates; extrinsics transform world coordinates into the camera frame. Lens-distortion coefficients model departures from ideal pinhole projection. [1](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d9/d0c/group__calib3d.html)

$$s\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\\1\end{pmatrix}=K[R\mid t]\begin{pmatrix}X\\Y\\Z\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad K=\begin{pmatrix}f_x&s_k&c_x\\0&f_y&c_y\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Radial distortion changes position with radius from the optical axis; tangential distortion captures decentering effects. Calibration fits these using known geometry and multiple views, then checks reprojection error and held-out views. Coordinate conventions, units, resizing/cropping, and rolling shutter matter. A low average reprojection error does not guarantee reliable extrapolation to image corners or a different focus/zoom setting; retain calibration conditions and uncertainty.
